RR Auction has concluded the auction of the late Apple founder Steve Jobs' 1968 science fair project, with the handmade exhibit ultimately selling for $34,375. Details are as follows.

"Overall condition is very good to excellent"

Previously, we reported that a science fair project created by Jobs in 1968, when he was in the second year of high school, was up for auction.

The project focused on a silicon-controlled rectifier, accompanied by two demonstration circuits and a 10-page report. At the time, online bidding had not yet reached $3,000.

The auction was part of "Steve Jobs & the Computer Revolution: The Apple 50th Anniversary Auction Part Two." Bidding has now closed, and MacRumors first reported that the final sale price reached $34,375.

According to RR Auction, the exhibit "had been kept at the famous 'Apple garage' property for many years" and was well preserved by Jobs' family. Jobs' step-brother, John Chovanec, said that Jobs repeatedly refused to take the exhibit back, ultimately allowing Chovanec to keep it.

"Steve Jobs & the Computer Revolution: The Apple 50th Anniversary Auction Part Two" featured nearly 150 Apple- and tech-related treasures, including a business card personally signed by Jobs, a collection of electronic components personally owned by Jobs, and a letter in which he declined a speaking invitation in 1983. These sold for $156,658, $27,188, and $24,695 respectively.

The highest-selling item in this auction was a fully working Apple-1 computer from the second batch of 50 produced, which sold for $499,363.

Do you have a precious Apple collectible in your possession? Feel free to let us know in the comments section.
